title: Training errors and running related injuries: a systematic review
authors: Nielsen RO, Buist I, Sorensen H, Lind M, Rasmussen S
journal: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
population: Novice, recreational or elite runners aged 18-65 in 31 studies (9 retrospective cohort, 13 prospective cohort, 6 case-control, 3 RCT)
findings: 4561 titles and abstracts were examined and 63 articles identified as potentially relevant; 31 studies were finally included.
Conflicting results were reported on the relationships between volume, duration, intensity and frequency and RRI.
Authors conclude it was not possible to identify which training errors relate to running-related injuries.
After examining 4561 titles and abstracts, 63 articles were potentially relevant; 31 studies were included (9 retrospective cohort, 13 prospective cohort, 6 case-control, 3 RCTs).
The authors concluded it was not possible to identify which training errors were related to running-related injuries.
limitations: Low mean study quality; heterogeneous exposure measurement; predates GPS-based cohorts (Nielsen 2014, Frandsen 2025); no DOI is registered for this record (IJSPT 2012 7(1):58-75), verified through PubMed and PMC instead.
implications: No volume, frequency or intensity 'training error' threshold was empirically established as of 2012, so the engine should label progression limits as conservative defaults.
Do not claim a validated causal link between any single training variable and injury.
Treat any single training-load rule (10% rule, mileage caps, intensity caps) as unproven; present as defaults, not as injury-prevention guarantees.
Prefer monitoring plus individual response (pain, load tolerance) over rigid population-level load thresholds.
